comparability.reason: All single-use polystyrene resins were operated in the same field pilot system, in parallel columns with identical groundwater influent, EBCT, and bed configuration; endpoints are expressed as bed volumes to PFAS breakthrough, allowing conditional comparison across resins and PFAS analytes.

endpoints.interpretation: Continuous-flow removal of PFASs by single-use polystyrene-based anion exchange resins, characterized by bed volumes treated until breakthrough of individual PFASs and by non-detect effluent concentrations for long-chain PFSAs over extended operation.
endpoints.reported_term: PFAS breakthrough and bed volumes treated

endpoints.interpretation: Postmortem analysis showed higher total PFAS mass adsorbed in the first section of the single-use resin columns, with decreasing adsorbed mass along the column length, indicating chromatographic-like sorption front development under competitive multisolute conditions.
endpoints.reported_term: PFAS adsorption profiles along column

limitations.statement: Pilot was conducted at a single high-concentration AFFF-impacted groundwater site, so performance and bed volumes to breakthrough may not directly generalize to lower-concentration or compositionally different sites.

Authors state that other factors beyond maximum adsorption capacity measured in batch equilibrium experiments control PFAS uptake and competition in continuous flow, implying limited predictive power of batch maximum capacity for field breakthrough.

Empirical correlations between batch-derived exchange coefficients and 50% breakthrough bed volumes are suggested as promising but are noted to require further validation before being used for prediction of new resins’ field performance.

comparability.reason: This study provides batch equilibrium isotherm data and qualitative assessments of how source water characteristics affect PFAS adsorption to GAC, but it does not report column, pilot, or full-scale breakthrough, bed volumes, or media lifetime. Batch conditions, ground GAC, and the absence of flow and bed-structure information mean that the results are useful for qualitative comparison and for informing models, but they are not directly comparable on a quantitative basis with continuous-treatment performance metrics.

endpoints.interpretation: Equilibrium batch isotherm tests quantified PFAS uptake by GAC as a function of equilibrium PFAS concentration, to derive adsorption capacities and isotherm parameters and to assess how source water characteristics (NOM, competing PFAS, ions, pH) affect capacity. These measurements address sorption behavior rather than column breakthrough or destruction.

endpoints.interpretation: While the study discusses GAC “treatment efficacy,” the actual experiments measured equilibrium adsorption capacities and removal in batch, not continuous-treatment breakthrough; removal is therefore interpreted as batch-phase PFAS concentration decrease at equilibrium, conditional on the isotherm tests.

endpoints.interpretation: The study evaluates the suitability and limitations of applying ideal adsorbed solution theory (IAST) and AdDesignS-type models for predicting PFAS mixture adsorption from batch isotherm data, highlighting that PFAS trace-level behavior and competition can lead to modeling inaccuracies when scaling to column performance.
endpoints.reported_term: modeling performance of IAST and column-scale design assumptions

limitations.statement: Isotherm (batch) tests do not directly evaluate adsorption breakthrough in GAC columns; modeling tools (e.g., Adsorption Design Software) are required to relate isotherm parameters to full- or pilot-scale breakthrough performance.

Isotherm parameters obtained with ground GAC may need adjustment when used to design or model full- or pilot-scale GAC systems with larger particle sizes, due to particle-size impacts on adsorption behavior and kinetics.

Ideal adsorbed solution theory (IAST) performed poorly for PFAS mixtures, with and without NOM, and may be insensitive when modeling trace constituents like PFAS; using IAST as currently implemented can therefore lead to errors in predicting GAC performance from batch data.

The study focused on impacts of NOM and major ions and did not investigate competition with non-PFAS adsorbable synthetic organic compounds; additional background species and kinetics in columns were not explored.

Because the work uses controlled batch isotherm experiments rather than site-specific pilot or full-scale columns, results can indicate general trends but cannot replace site-specific pilot or other studies to determine actual GAC breakthrough performance.

Only bench-scale, batch equilibrium conditions were investigated; no flow, bed configuration, or real-time breakthrough data were collected, which limits direct translation to media lifetime or bed volumes treated in continuous systems.

endpoints.interpretation: PFAS breakthrough curves in RSSCT columns were used to evaluate apparent adsorption capacity and to test whether intraparticle diffusion depended on particle size. Similar PFAS breakthrough trends for three different F400 particle sizes at the same EBCT indicated that intraparticle diffusion was independent of particle size, supporting use of the constant diffusivity (CD) model for scaling RSSCTs to pilot- or full-scale fixed-bed adsorbers.

limitations.statement: Pilot-scale testing best represents full-scale fixed-bed GAC adsorbers because it accounts for heterogeneity of adsorbent sizes and pore blocking by dissolved organic matter, which are difficult to simulate with bench-scale RSSCTs or numerical simulations.

It is practically challenging to use pilot-testing to design a full-scale fixed-bed adsorber because of the extended timeframe required to generate a full breakthrough profile, especially for long-chain hydrophobic PFAS.

Although F400 particle size had negligible influence on PFAS breakthrough under the study conditions, the dependency of PFAS breakthrough on adsorbent size could differ in pilot- or full-scale systems during long-term operation due to pore blocking.

Numerical simulations for predicting full-scale PFAS breakthrough require estimation of kinetic parameters (mass transfer, surface diffusion, pore diffusion coefficients), and the predictive capability is highly dependent on parameter estimation quality.

endpoints.interpretation: Breakthrough curves for PFBA, PFPeA, and PFHxA were analyzed at three EBCT_LC values (5, 10, 20 min) to understand how EBCT affects apparent adsorption capacity and mass transfer zone development. PFBA, the most weakly adsorbing PFAS, showed shallower breakthrough as EBCT increased, indicating greater mass transfer zone development, while PFPeA and PFHxA showed less pronounced differences among EBCTs. Longer EBCTs produced steeper breakthroughs with respect to bed volumes for F400 but similar BV50, implying that EBCT strongly affects breakthrough curve shape and overshoot behavior rather than apparent capacity.

endpoints.interpretation: Half breakthrough bed volume (BV50) for F400 was used as an indicator of apparent adsorption capacity. BV50 showed a monotonic correlation with PFAS Log Dow at the experimental pH, indicating that hydrophobic interactions primarily determine apparent adsorption capacity for F400. Overshoot in effluent concentrations due to chromatographic effects was observed for more hydrophilic PFAS (PFBA, PFPeA), especially at longer EBCTs. An empirical equation relating BV10 to PFAS hydrophobicity and/or other parameters was developed to predict bed volumes to 10% breakthrough, providing a design-oriented performance metric for continuous systems from RSSCT data.

limitations.statement: The empirical equation obtained for predicting BV10 is based on RSSCT data for specific PFAS and GACs in groundwater; applicability to other PFAS mixtures, water matrices, and GAC types may be limited without further validation.

Chromatographic overshoot of hydrophilic PFAS (PFBA, PFPeA) complicates interpretation of breakthrough curves and may lead to under- or over-estimation of apparent capacity if simple breakthrough criteria are used.

comparability.reason: The model explicitly links batch-derived sorption and kinetic parameters to predicted full-scale GAC breakthrough for multiple PFASs in AFFF-impacted water, with defined vessel volume, bed depth, and flow rate. However, predictions are qualitative and contingent on assumptions about intraparticle diffusion, DOC fouling, and competitive sorption; thus, comparisons to actual column or plant performance are valid only when these conditions are similar.

endpoints.interpretation: The model used batch-calibrated sorption and diffusion parameters to predict PFAS breakthrough in a full-scale GAC system, reporting bed volumes to breakthrough and comparing predicted breakthrough order across PFASs to previous column observations.

endpoints.interpretation: Relative PFAS sorptive affinity derived from batch Kd values was used to predict relative breakthrough order in columns; both equilibrium and diffusion-limited models produced similar breakthrough orders for most PFASs, suggesting that batch-derived affinity may qualitatively indicate breakthrough sequence when column tests are not feasible.
endpoints.reported_term: relative affinity; breakthrough order

limitations.statement: The forward-modeling approach provides useful qualitative insight into PFAS breakthrough behavior, but the authors recommend that pilot-scale column verification experiments be conducted when sufficient water quantities are available.

Competition for sorption sites (between PFASs and between PFASs and dissolved organic carbon) may affect breakthrough behavior differently in actual systems than predicted by the model, particularly under continuous DOC loading and potential GAC fouling.

A previous application of the same model indicated that batch calibration experiments at higher DOC levels improved prediction of column breakthrough, suggesting that the present model may underrepresent DOC fouling effects when extrapolating from batch data.

Apparent tortuosity was treated as an adjustable parameter to fit PFAS-specific kinetic behavior, rather than being independently measured, which may limit the mechanistic interpretability and transferability of the calibrated model parameters.

Pilot results and model fits are specific to a particular groundwater quality and PFAS mixture, limiting direct generalization to other waters without additional validation.

comparability.reason: PD-RSSCTs, pilot-scale, and full-scale GAC systems used the same adsorbent type and similar water matrices, and performance was evaluated using consistent endpoints (bed volumes to 10% and 50% breakthrough), providing a direct basis to compare bench-scale predictions with continuous-flow column behavior. However, differences in particle size, hydrodynamics, and fouling imply that comparability is conditional and requires correction factors.

endpoints.interpretation: PD-RSSCT breakthrough curves were compared with full-scale GW and pilot-scale SW breakthrough curves in terms of bed volumes to 10% and 50% PFAA breakthrough. For MN GW, PD-RSSCTs consistently overpredicted full-scale PFAA adsorption capacity (bed volumes to breakthrough) by an average factor of about 1.7 (range 1.4–2.0). For NC SW, PD-RSSCTs matched pilot-scale PFAA breakthrough more closely, indicating better predictive performance in this matrix. Batch tests showed that two GACs had similar PFAA removal in GW, but the GAC with larger mesopore volume was more effective in SW.
endpoints.reported_term: Adsorption capacity / bed volumes to 10% and 50% breakthrough in PD-RSSCT vs full- and pilot-scale GAC adsorbers

limitations.statement: PD-RSSCTs consistently overpredicted full-scale PFAA adsorption capacity in groundwater by an average factor of 1.7 (range 1.4–2.0), demonstrating that unadjusted PD-RSSCT data do not reliably predict full-scale performance for PFAAs in this matrix.

Pore blockage near the external GAC surface by dissolved organic matter in larger full-scale GAC particles is proposed as the strongest working hypothesis for the observed overprediction, implying that particle-size-dependent fouling effects are not fully captured by RSSCT design assumptions.
Bench-scale batch and RSSCT experiments were conducted with specific GW and SW matrices and two coal-based GACs, so extrapolation to other PFAS, waters, or carbon types should be made cautiously.

Although PD-RSSCT performance for NC SW matched pilot-scale breakthrough curves more closely than for MN GW, detailed quantitative prediction errors for SW were not provided in the extracted text, limiting assessment of predictive uncertainty in that matrix.

The described endpoint is bed volumes to 10% and 50% breakthrough and associated adsorption capacity/throughput comparisons between RSSCT and full-/pilot-scale systems (S13-E01, S13-E02, S13-E04, S13-E07). This is a capacity/throughput endpoint, not a direct removal fraction. Classifying endpoint_type as 'removal' misrepresents the measured basis and is not directly supported by the cited text.

The interpretation states that PD-RSSCT breakthrough curves were compared with full- and pilot-scale curves in terms of bed volumes to 10% and 50% breakthrough, that PD-RSSCTs overpredicted full-scale performance in MN GW by a mean factor of 1.7 (range 1.4–2.0), that the NC SW PD-RSSCT matched pilot-scale curves more closely, and that batch tests showed similar PFAA removal by two GACs in GW but better performance of the higher-mesopore-volume GAC in SW.
